newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Defiant Netanyahu rejects UN settlement decision.
newsitem.headline: Defiant Netanyahu rejects UN settlement decision.

text.p: A defiant Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected a U.N. condemnation of his Jewish settlement policy, vowing to remain unswayed by international pressure no matter "what they will say about us in the world".
The U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday approved by overwhelming vote a resolution urging member states to actively discourage the building of Jewish settlements in occupied areas.

"There are things more important than what they will say about us in the world, and Jerusalem stands at the head of these things, and we will not surrender to any pressures on this subject," Netanyahu was quoted as telling cabinet ministers, in a statement released by his office late on Wednesday.
The General Assembly vote was 131-3 with 14 abstentions. Israel, Micronesia and the United States voted against.

The resolution, sponsored by 15 Arab and Moslem nations, followed a report by U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan condemning Israel for not abandoning settlement construction at a site in Arab East Jerusalem called Har Homa by Israelis and Jabal Abu Ghneim by Arabs.
The start of construction last March plunged Israel-PLO peacemaking into crisis and triggered waves of Arab unrest in the West Bank and Gaza, captured in the 1967 Middle East War.

The Israeli army, anxious to reduce friction ahead of Moslem commemorations of the Prophet Mohammad's birthdate on Thursday, declared off-limits to Israelis all PLO-ruled West Bank cities and Hebron's al-Ibrahimi mosque, a shrine sacred to Moslems and Jews as the site of the tomb of the biblical Abraham.
As a further step, the army early on Thursday reopened two streets it had blockaded during recent clashes in the heart of Hebron.
Hebron has been ravaged by violence since last month, when a Jewish woman put up posters there depicting Mohammad as a pig.

In the West Bank town of Bethlehem Palestinians hurled firebombs and stones at Israeli troops after hundreds of supporters of the militant Moslem Hamas marched in a funeral procession for an activist killed this week when a bomb he was assembling exploded in his hands, Palestinians said.

In a lone vestige of Israeli-PLO talks, Palestinian senior official Nabil Shaath met Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai on Wednesday night in the latest in a series of meetings under the auspices of the Egyptian and U.S. ambassadors to Israel.
Shaath and Mordechai were expected to discuss confidence-building measures, specifically an airport to serve Palestinians in the self-ruled Gaza Strip.
"I'm not that optimistic, but I keep hoping we will do something to save this peace process," Shaath told Reuters before the meeting.

Foreign Minister David Levy said the U.N. resolution was intended "to isolate Israel, to hurt it, and even to propose its being ejected from the United Nations". Netanyahu aide David Bar-Illan criticised the vote as "shameful" and "morally bankrupt".
The Assembly demanded at an emergency special session in April that Israel halt work at the Jerusalem site, where bulldozers are preparing the infrastructure for 6,500 homes.

Palestinians, who had lobbied vigorously for the resolution, applauded the Tuesday U.N. vote. Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said in Gaza that the decision "gives the proof that all the world is against what the Israelis are doing".

The fate of Jerusalem is at the heart of the conflict, but the "final status" talks which were to have settled this and other core issues by 1999 were rendered stillborn by the rise to power of Netanyahu's hardline government in June, 1996.
Israel, which captured East Jerusalem in 1967 and later annexed it in a move the international community has not recognised, says all of Jerusalem is its united capital.

Arabs view the Jerusalem construction and other settlement activity as an attempt to pre-empt future peace talks on the West Bank, viewed by Palestinians as part of a future state with its capital in East Jerusalem.
